transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2028-11-08 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (OpalWorks), Luca Romano (OpalWorks), Maya Patel (OpalWorks), Ethan Brooks (OpalWorks)

Summary (auto): short discovery. customer has strict egress and APAC residency needs, wants private-only deployment with host in their VPC or peered private endpoints.

[00:00] Avery (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Avery with Redwood, this is Diego our solutions engineer. quick intro round?
[00:08] Priya (OpalWorks): Hi Priya here, Head of Cloud Platform. we run multi-account AWS, some GCP for analytics.
[00:12] Luca: Luca, infra eng, i'll be the hands on keyboard for network stuff.
[00:15] Maya: Maya, security, i'll be focused on compliance and egress controls.
[00:18] Ethan: Ethan, SRE, interested in latency and failover.
[00:21] Avery: Cool. high level we want to understand your constraints for a private deployment - VPC peering, private endpoints, Transit Gateway, regions. Diego will talk architecture patterns, then we can dive into your specific CIDRs and egress.
[00:32] Diego (Redwood SE): Thanks. so Redwood Private can be run two ways: we provide private endpoints in your VPC (private Link-style) or we deploy in a customer-managed VPC via a small set of instances/containers that we manage. the common patterns are: 1) VPC peering for small setups, 2) Transit Gateway for multi-account multi-region, or 3) PrivateLink endpoints if you want minimal routing changes. each has tradeoffs on IP space and route table changes.
[01:05] Priya: For us we have many accounts under an org and a centralized transit hub. Prefer not to peer every account, TGW already in place. also APAC data residency is critical — some customers must stay in ap-southeast-1 or ap-northeast-1.
[01:22] Diego: TGW is a good fit. with TGW we can attach a Redwood VPC or the Redwood managed connectors to your transit and advertise routes. you'd typically allocate a small subnet for private endpoints, /28 or /27 depending on scale. note: our private endpoints need stable IPs for firewall allow-lists.
[01:39] Luca: Wait, /27 for endpoints? how many IPs do you need per environment? we need to plan prefixes carefully because our CIDR planning is tight.
[01:45] Diego: yeah — for a single environment and small pilot, /28 (16 addresses, 11 usable) often suffices. production at scale we'd recommend /26 or /25 depending on concurrency. also we have ephemeral workload IPs for the inference workers, those sit behind NAT if you require egress through your firewall.
[02:06] Maya: about egress: our policy is all outbound traffic must go through our corporate egress proxy and firewall. can Redwood use our egress for outgoing requests, or does it need to egress to the internet from your side?
[02:16] Avery: good question. Redwood Private can be configured so that outbound egress exits via your VPC NAT/egress (we can route through your firewall). alternatively, in a fully-hosted Redwood scenario egress goes out of our managed subnet. seems you want customer-controlled egress.
[02:31] Ethan: latency is important for some endpoints. if traffic has to hairpin through a proxy, are there latency numbers we should expect?
[02:36] Diego: hairpinning through corporate proxies adds variable latency — for us the main path is client -> your proxy -> Redwood endpoints. Usually adds 20-70ms depending on proxy, it depends on path to the region. For the APAC region we'd recommend deploying in ap-southeast-1 to reduce RTT.
[02:55] Priya: we also have compliance asks: SOC2, ISO, audit logs, KMS integration for keys. can you accept our KMS or do you use your own?
[03:04] Avery: Redwood supports customer-managed KMS for Private deployments; we can integrate with your KMS or HSM. we'll include our current SOC2/ISO docs in the security pack.
[03:13] Maya: ok. another point — IP allow lists, and TLS mutual auth for control plane? we prefer mTLS for service-to-service.
[03:20] Diego: we support mTLS for sensitive control-plane channels and can terminate TLS at your side if that's required. for data plane traffic, mutual TLS is possible with certificate exchange. we would work through certificate management with your security team.
[03:34] Luca: can you walk through the TGW route table changes? we run segmented route tables per account for compliance, don't want to open everything.
[03:42] Diego: sure. typical pattern is to attach a dedicated Redwood VPC to the TGW, then advertise only the private endpoint CIDRs to the hub. You keep granular route tables — only the accounts you want will route to Redwood. we do not require full mesh peering. We can also use Transit Gateway route table propagation so you can control propagation scope.
[04:05] Priya: Do you have a diagram for that?
[04:07] Avery: yes we'll include a couple of diagrams: TGW attach, PrivateLink option, and a model where we host a small footprint in your VPC.
[04:15] Ethan: what about IP exhaustion? we have /16s per environment but some teams carved small /24s; giving up /26 is tough.
[04:24] Diego: understood — smallest footprint is PrivateLink which only needs a handful of IPs in the service consumer subnets. If you can't spare /28s in the hub, we can host the connector in a Redwood-managed account and advertise routes to your hub — that requires trusting our attach but reduces the need for your IPs.
[04:42] Maya: that sounds like a trust boundary we need to evaluate. can we do a canary where limited data flows and we capture audit logs?
[04:49] Avery: absolutely — pilot with scoped traffic and strict telemetry. Redwood Console provides per-token latency and cost breakdowns and will stream logs to your SIEM or S3.
[05:01] Priya: about regions — some customers specifically require processing in Singapore region only. do you support per-region deployments?
[05:08] Diego: yes, we support region pinning. we can deploy dedicated capacity in ap-southeast-1. for Private, we either deploy connectors in that region or use your TGW to reach our regional connector. Key point: data residency plus low latency -> deploy regionally.
[05:22] Priya: cost tradeoffs — if we go regional dedicated vs hosted, what's the cost delta?
[05:27] Avery: hosted is generally lower immediate ops cost, but dedicated/reserved capacity gives predictable throughput pricing and lower per-token cost at scale. We'll provide a cost estimate based on token throughput in the pilot.
[05:38] Luca: network ACLs and security groups — do you require specific SGs on our side?
[05:42] Diego: we'll provide a small set: allow inbound from your management CIDR to the private endpoint ports (HTTPS 443), some health-check ports, and we publish the IPs that must be allowed.
[05:53] Maya: are there any AWS service endpoints we need to enable? PrivateLink uses AWS PrivateLink endpoints, but do you depend on S3 or others?
[06:01] Diego: We rely on S3 for model artifacts in some private deployments. If you want everything internal, we can copy artifacts into your S3 buckets and reference them directly, or we can pull from Redwood S3. We'll document both options.
[06:14] Priya: ok. let's talk timeline for POC. We're aiming for a short pilot for eval in mid-November, can we do a 3-week pilot?
[06:22] Avery: yes that's reasonable. typical pilot steps: kickoff, network setup (we exchange CIDRs and SGs), deploy connectors, run benchmark jobs with your sample prompts, and capture metrics.
[06:34] Ethan: benchmark — what workload should we run to measure cost/latency? we have a mix of short chat queries and long completion requests.
[06:40] Diego: we'll suggest a prompt set. short completions (10-40 tokens) and longer ones (200-600 tokens) to model KV-cache warmup. We'll also run sustained throughput tests to validate the autoscale.
[06:53] Priya: do you offer quantization or lower precision models to reduce GPU usage?
[06:58] Avery: Redwood Optimize provides quantization recommendations; for Private you can pick a quantized model variant to reduce cost at some quality tradeoff. we'll include suggestions based on sample evals.
[07:10] Luca: networking — one more question: for cross-region failover, do you recommend active-active or active-passive?
[07:16] Diego: active-active can be done but requires session affinity considerations due to KV caches. Many customers do active-passive for deterministic behavior, with fallback routes in TGW to a secondary region. We'll help configure sticky routing if you need active-active.
[07:31] Maya: log retention and audit — how long do you keep logs in your console? we need 365 days for certain customers.
[07:36] Avery: Redwood Console retention is configurable; enterprise/private customers can set long-term retention or stream to your S3/SIEM for compliance.
[07:47] Priya: any blockers on our end to get started? we'll need the security pack and an initial IP plan.
[07:53] Avery: action items noted — we'll send security pack and sample diagrams. Diego will prepare TGW routing examples.
[07:59] Luca: i'll share our VPC CIDRs and the TGW route table and a minimal ACL example.
[08:04] Maya: i'll confirm data residency constraints for APAC customer list and share any regulatory checklists.
[08:09] Avery: perfect. quick recap before we close?
[08:12] Diego: recap: configuration options (PrivateLink, TGW attach, connector-in-customer-VPC), IP sizing guidance (/28 for pilot), customer-controlled egress possible, KMS integration and mTLS supported, region pinning for APAC, pilot timeline target mid-November for three weeks.
[08:34] Priya: that matches our needs, thanks.
[08:36] Avery: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs and calendar invites for the deep dive.
[08:41] Priya: thanks, bye.

Notes on transcription quality: some technical terms were auto-transcribed as similar-sounding words (e.g., "K-V cash" for KV cache, "Transit way" for Transit Gateway). Speaker attribution occasionally simplified.
